sourceSpan.excerpt: Now, tonight's topic, does God exist? All right. Well, I believe he does. But let me make it clear that I'm not arguing for the generic existence of any kind of a God concept, but only the God of the Bible. I am an ordained minister. I'm a Trinitarian who believes in salvation that can be found only through the person and work of Jesus, who, according to the scriptures, is God in flesh, who died on the cross for our sins, and rose from the dead 3 days later. Since I believe this, and I take the affirmative position in our debate, then the burden is upon me to at least try and demonstrate that God exists. But in order to do this, I'm not going to do it the wrong way. I won't put on a lab coat. I won't produce a microscope, get an X-ray machine in order to try and detect God's existence through some experimentation, some procedures. This is the wrong approach because scientific methodology is designed to detect, repeat, and explain phenomena in the material world, not the world outside of it. It is not designed to detect existence or the existence of a divine person who transcends it. Now, think about it. Do you know of any person who behaves in a a mechanistic, naturalistic, predictable fashion? Cuz God is a person. Or are there aspects of irregularity, unpredictability, and variableness in their behavior due to them being persons that don't fit in the scientific method? Let me just tell you, going to the scientific method to try and find God is the wrong approach. In my article on my website, carm.org, "What Kind of Evidence Should We Expect From a Transcendent God?" I say, quote, "Since a transcendent God who created the universe would not be limited to it, but would transcend it, then we can expect that evidence for God's existence would share transcendent characteristics." Close quote. Therefore, if we encounter transcendent characteristics in the world, then we have encountered evidence for God's existence.

sourceSpan.excerpt: Well, I agree that logic is a function of the brain, but not just the brain. We both know that people can reason correctly. But how would you recognize correct reasoning if not by appealing to something outside the brain, such as the laws of logic, which guide proper reasoning? But these laws cannot be the product of the human brain. Otherwise, there is no way to determine if a person's reasoning is right or wrong. When the brain functions logically, it must be in harmony with the laws of logic. When the brain functions illogically, then it is not in harmony with those laws. But those laws are external to and independent of the brain since they govern it in regard to proper reasoning. Furthermore, the laws of logic are special kinds of propositions they since they are about truth. And that's one reason we know they require a mind because no material thing can be about another thing. Truth statements require minds.

sourceSpan.excerpt: How does the atheistic perspective account for these laws? If the laws of logic are just functions of the human brain, as Mr. Barker stated, then that explanation cannot work because brains are different, and people contradict each other. Furthermore, if someone's physical brain causes him to deny the law of non-contradiction, that law is not invalidated. It's still true. Therefore, this proves that the logical thinking occurs in the brain, and the laws of logic do not depend upon human brains for their validity. If these logical laws are agreed-upon principles that people recognize as true, then they are recognizing principles that already exist. But how is it possible to have preexistent logical propositions in an atheistic worldview? And if it is people who declare these axioms to be true, then do the logical propositions become untrue when people decide they don't serve their subjective wants anymore? If these laws of logic are descriptions of natural phenomena, then how do you, for example, observe the law of proper inference in nature, which says if A equals B and B equals C, then A equals C without first presupposing the validity of the laws of logic which you used to deduce its truth. To do so is to beg the question. If these laws of logic are said to be properties of the universe, then they should be measurable since properties of the physical realm are quantifiable, whether they be things such as hardness, mass, polarity, or density. But you cannot apply this to the laws of logic. Furthermore, these laws of logic are characteristics that contain universality. They're true for everyone all the time. If you don't agree with the law of logic, the law of non-contradiction, it doesn't make it go away. We know that when people contradict themselves, we know they're just wrong. But these laws are there. They're not just a function of the brain. And they have a universality to them. They have a quality that applies to everyone all the time. They transcend it space and time. They have a transcendent characteristic. Now, which worldview best provides the rational justification for these transcendent universal truths? If the is Oh, man. Sorry. Is it the Christian worldview that proposes a transcendent mind that is the Christian God and who has revealed these universally true laws which are reflections of his perfect transcendent mind? Or are they the product of human brain action via evolution that assigned universal truth principles in the physical world and asserts them as a function of the physical brain? I assert that it's the former which makes sense and the atheistic perspective does not and cannot.

sourceSpan.excerpt: If the universe had a beginning, then it brought itself into existence or it did not bring itself into existence. Since nothing comes from nothing, unless you're into magic and children's imaginations, then we can conclude that the universe did not cause itself to exist. Instead, it was caused to exist by something other than itself. There are only two options to account for this cause, personal and non-personal. There's no third option. So let's look at the impersonal cause, the atheistic cause. An impersonal cause of the universe had to exist prior to the universe. Since time appears to be a function of the physical realm, the prior cause must have existed in a timeless state. This cause must also have had the necessary sufficient conditions to bring the universe into existence. But if it was a an impersonal cause that possessed the necessary sufficient conditions, then the resultant creation would have been automatic. Let me illustrate. If I want to move a boulder with a lever, I would need both the necessary and sufficient conditions. The necessary conditions would be the boulder, the ground, a fulcrum, a lever, and a counterweight. But if one of those necessary conditions is not sufficient, say the counterweight is not heavy enough, then the boulder will not move. But as soon as all the necessary conditions are also sufficient, which includes the counterweight being heavy enough, the result in this impersonal arrangement is automatic. The boulder moves. But if we add a personable variable, say a person's ability to pull the lever when she decides to, then the result occurs when she decides it will occur. Now, if there were an impersonal cause that also possessed the necessary and sufficient conditions to create the universe, then the creation would necessarily have been automatic. Since the impersonal cause existed for lack of better term forever, then the universe would have been brought into existence automatically an infinitely long time ago. But this is not the case. Since the universe is not infinitely old, then it is not possible that an impersonal cause brought the universe into existence an infinitely long time ago. A something that would create the universe had to exist in a timeless state before it and unchanging, but it had to have the necessary sufficient conditions. It automatically would have occurred infinitely long time ago, which means the universe would be infinitely old, but it's not. So therefore that can't work. It makes more sense to say that there was a personal cause that contained both the necessary and sufficient conditions and that any particular moment of his choosing decided to say, "Let there be light." and the universe came into existence. In the case of the creation of the universe, this would mean that the personal being transcends the universe itself and is the cause of it and decided to create it at a particular point in the time past. Hence, another example of transcendence.
